messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos walked into the therapist’s office with the careful deliberation of a man who had spent decades scanning every room before he entered. At sixty-five, divorced, and still working as a special education teacher in a Chicago public school, he carried a past that had never been just the past. The traumatic event that had shaped him happened during his first deployment in the Vietnam War, when he was twenty-two. His unit came under mortar fire near a river; the explosion threw him face-first into muddy water, and when he came up gasping, the taste of silt and gasoline filled his mouth. For years afterward, the same metallic, earthy taste could rise without warning, especially when he felt dizzy—a symptom that first appeared after a mild concussion from the blast but had never fully disappeared. Dizziness itself became a kind of trigger, because every time the room seemed to tilt, his throat filled again with that phantom taste, and he was back in the mud, waiting for the next round.

Over the decades, Carlos had learned to live with these intrusions by constructing a careful system of control. For example, a conversation about the war—even a casual one with a fellow teacher during lunch—could bring on both the taste and a wave of lightheadedness, so he had come to believe that strong emotions of any kind were dangerous. He avoided emotional stress by pulling away from arguments, from celebrations, from anything that might stir him too deeply. In his classroom, he always chose a desk near the door, and when he took his students to the cafeteria or the playground, he positioned himself so that he could see every exit. This constant checking of his surroundings was not a choice; it was a reflex born from years of scanning for signs of threat, a vigilance that had hardened into a permanent way of moving through the world.

The threat monitoring itself was relentless. Carlos noted that when he heard unexpected loud sounds—a book slamming, a fire drill alarm, a car backfiring—his heart would hammer and he would freeze, then automatically begin calculating the nearest escape route. This planning had become second nature. In a restaurant or a movie theater, he could not sit until he had located every door and window, mentally rehearsing the quickest path to safety. The paradox was that this very vigilance made the triggers more frequent. The hypervigilance itself—the scanning, the tensing at noises—could bring on a wave of dizziness, because his body was always bracing for something. And once the dizziness started, the taste would follow, and then he would feel compelled to check his surroundings even more obsessively, which only heightened his alertness. A loop tightened around him: the threat of dizziness led him to scan, the scanning made him dizzy, and the dizziness brought the taste, which sent him back into survival mode.

This cycle had cost him. His marriage, already strained by his emotional withdrawal, ended after fifteen years. His ex-wife had told him she could not live with someone who flinched at her touch and jumped at every sound. Carlos understood, though he never said so. At work, he managed well enough because he had structured his life around his routines: he taught the same way each day, avoided discussing his past, and kept his students in a predictable, low-stimulation environment. But a few weeks ago, a student unexpectedly burst into tears during a reading exercise—a sudden, sharp sound that made Carlos jump and then, as the taste rose and the room tilted, he had to excuse himself to the bathroom, where he stayed until the dizziness passed. That incident, and another when a gustatory memory surfaced without any obvious trigger while he was driving home, convinced him that his strategies were failing. He had come for help because he was afraid, but he could not say exactly of what—only that the danger he had been watching for his whole life had never shown itself, and he was tired of watching.
